words.definition: a material, organism or environmental feature that people use or value
words.example: Forests provide timber, food, recreation and climate regulation as natural resources.

words.definition: a resource replenished naturally on a timescale comparable with human use if managed appropriately
words.example: A sustainably managed forest can function as a renewable resource.

words.definition: a resource formed so slowly that stocks are effectively finite on human timescales
words.example: Crude oil is a non-renewable resource.

words.definition: a resource that can recover through natural processes but may be depleted if use exceeds renewal
words.example: Groundwater may be replenishable where recharge is rapid enough.

words.definition: stocks of natural assets that provide resources and ecosystem services
words.example: Wetlands are natural capital because they store water and support biodiversity.

words.definition: the renewable goods and services generated by natural capital over time
words.example: A sustainably harvested fish catch is a form of natural income.

words.definition: a benefit people obtain from functioning ecosystems
words.example: Flood regulation by wetlands is an ecosystem service.

words.definition: a material product obtained from ecosystems, such as food, water or timber
words.example: Crop production is a provisioning service.

words.definition: a benefit arising from ecosystem regulation of processes such as climate, floods or disease
words.example: Mangroves provide a regulating service by reducing coastal erosion.

words.definition: a non-material benefit from ecosystems such as recreation, identity or spiritual value
words.example: National parks provide cultural services through tourism and recreation.

words.definition: a fundamental ecological process that underpins other ecosystem services
words.example: Nutrient cycling is often described as a supporting service.

words.definition: the quantity of a resource stored or available at a given time
words.example: Known mineral reserves form part of a resource stock.

words.definition: the rate at which a resource moves, is produced or is extracted from a stock
words.example: Annual timber harvest is a resource flow from a forest stock.

words.definition: the amount of a renewable resource that can be harvested without reducing its long-term productive capacity
words.example: Fishing below sustainable yield can help maintain a stock over time.

words.definition: a condition in which demand for a resource is high relative to accessible supply
words.example: Resource scarcity can increase prices and encourage substitution.

words.definition: replacement of one material or energy source with another that performs a similar function
words.example: Recycled aluminium can provide resource substitution for newly mined metal.

words.definition: reliable and affordable access to resources needed by a society
words.example: Diversifying energy sources can improve resource security.

words.definition: reduction in the quantity or quality of a resource through use or degradation
words.example: Excessive groundwater pumping causes resource depletion.

words.definition: planning and regulation of how resources are accessed, used, conserved and restored
words.example: Forest certification can support improved resource management.

words.definition: protection and efficient use of resources to reduce depletion and maintain future availability
words.example: Recycling metals can contribute to resource conservation.

words.definition: an energy-rich material such as coal, oil or natural gas formed from ancient organic matter
words.example: Burning fossil fuel releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants.

words.definition: a carbon-rich solid fossil fuel formed mainly from ancient plant material
words.example: Coal-fired power has high carbon dioxide emissions per unit of electricity.

words.definition: a liquid fossil fuel composed mainly of hydrocarbons and refined into fuels and chemicals
words.example: Oil is widely used for transport fuels and petrochemicals.

words.definition: a gaseous fossil fuel composed mainly of methane
words.example: Natural gas combustion emits less carbon dioxide than coal per unit of energy but methane leakage can be significant.

words.definition: energy released from changes in atomic nuclei, mainly fission in current power stations
words.example: Nuclear energy produces low operational carbon emissions but creates radioactive waste.

words.definition: a heavy radioactive element used as fuel in most nuclear fission reactors
words.example: Uranium must be mined and processed before use in a nuclear reactor.

words.definition: energy obtained from sunlight using technologies such as photovoltaic panels or solar thermal systems
words.example: Solar energy output varies with daylight and cloud cover.

words.definition: energy obtained by converting the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity
words.example: Wind farms generate electricity without fuel combustion.

words.definition: electricity generated by converting the energy of moving or falling water
words.example: Hydroelectricity can provide flexible power but large dams may alter river ecosystems.

words.definition: energy obtained from heat within Earth
words.example: Volcanically active regions often have high geothermal energy potential.

words.definition: energy derived from recently living organic material such as wood, crops or wastes
words.japanese: バイオマスエネルギー
words.example: Biomass energy can be renewable if harvesting does not exceed regrowth.

words.definition: energy generated from predictable movements of seawater caused by tides
words.example: Tidal energy has predictable timing but requires suitable coastal sites.

words.definition: energy captured from the motion of ocean surface waves
words.example: Wave energy devices are being tested in high-energy coastal environments.

words.definition: the combination and relative shares of energy sources used by a country or system
words.example: A country's energy mix may include coal, gas, nuclear and renewables.

words.definition: reliable, affordable and resilient access to sufficient energy supplies
words.example: Domestic renewable generation can improve energy security by reducing fuel imports.

words.definition: the actual energy produced by a power source compared with the maximum it could produce continuously
words.example: Wind turbines usually have lower capacity factors than nuclear plants.

words.definition: the ratio of usable energy obtained from an energy source to the energy required to obtain it
words.japanese: エネルギー投資収益率（EROI）
words.example: A high energy return on investment means relatively little energy is spent obtaining the energy supply.

words.definition: variation in output from an energy source because the resource is not continuously available
words.example: Solar power has intermittency because generation falls at night.

words.definition: technologies that store electricity or energy for later delivery to the power system
words.example: Battery grid storage can help balance variable renewable generation.

words.definition: a major structural shift from one set of energy sources and technologies to another
words.example: The move from fossil fuels toward low-carbon systems is an energy transition.

words.definition: everyday solid waste collected from households and similar commercial or institutional sources
words.example: Food scraps, packaging and discarded household items form municipal solid waste.

words.definition: discarded material capable of causing significant harm because it is toxic, corrosive, reactive or otherwise dangerous
words.example: Solvents and some industrial chemicals require special hazardous-waste treatment.

words.definition: discarded electrical or electronic devices and components
words.example: Electronic waste can contain valuable metals as well as toxic substances.

words.definition: edible or inedible food material discarded or lost along the supply chain
words.example: Reducing food waste can lower landfill methane and resource use.

words.definition: an engineered site where solid waste is deposited and buried
words.example: Modern landfills may collect leachate and methane.

words.definition: controlled burning of waste at high temperature
words.example: Incineration reduces waste volume but can create air emissions and ash.

words.definition: processing discarded materials so they can be used as raw materials again
words.example: Recycling aluminium generally requires less energy than producing primary metal.

words.definition: using a product or material again without major reprocessing
words.example: Refilling containers is a form of reuse.

words.definition: preventing waste by using fewer materials or consuming less
words.example: Choosing durable products can reduce waste generation.

words.definition: a ranking that prioritizes prevention, reuse and recycling over disposal
words.example: The waste hierarchy places prevention above landfill.

words.definition: controlled aerobic decomposition of organic waste into a soil-like material
words.example: Food and garden waste can be treated by composting.

words.definition: microbial breakdown of organic material without oxygen, producing biogas and digestate
words.example: Anaerobic digestion can turn food waste into methane-rich biogas.

words.definition: contaminated liquid formed when water passes through waste and dissolves or carries pollutants
words.example: Landfill liners help prevent leachate from entering groundwater.

words.definition: collection of methane produced by waste or other processes for treatment or energy use
words.example: Landfill methane capture can reduce greenhouse-gas emissions.

words.definition: the degree to which materials are kept in use through reduction, repair, reuse and recycling
words.example: Product redesign can improve circularity by making components easier to repair.

words.definition: a policy making producers financially or physically responsible for products after consumer use
words.example: Extended producer responsibility can require electronics companies to fund collection and recycling.

words.definition: systematic evaluation of environmental impacts across a product's stages from raw materials to disposal
words.japanese: ライフサイクルアセスメント
words.example: Life-cycle assessment can compare reusable and disposable packaging.

words.definition: design or marketing intended to shorten a product's useful life and encourage replacement
words.example: Planned obsolescence can increase material consumption and waste.

words.definition: a goal of preventing disposal by redesigning systems around reduction, reuse, repair and material recovery
words.example: A zero-waste strategy aims to minimize incineration and landfill.

words.definition: generation of usable energy from waste through processes such as combustion or anaerobic digestion
words.example: Waste-to-energy plants can produce electricity but may compete with recycling goals.
